  prepared cadet. Part (c) is the one that matters — a cadet who recomputes from scratch has the
  formula but not the scaling, and a cadet who divides by 3 has the wrong scaling entirely.

B — Counting the electrons, then feeling them
Statement: A plastic rod is rubbed with a cloth and ends up with a charge of -8.0 nC.
  (a) How many excess electrons are on the rod?
  (b) The cloth is measured and found to carry +8.0 nC. Explain why, and say how many electrons the
      cloth lost.
  (c) The rod and the cloth are then held 15 cm apart. Find the magnitude and direction of the
      electric force between them.
Worked answer (tutor reference only):
  Pass 1:
    (a) Charge is quantized, so the rod's charge is an integer multiple of e:
          N = |q| / e = 8.0e-9 C / 1.602e-19 C = 4.9938e10 electrons, so about 5.0e10.
    (b) The same 5.0e10 electrons. Nothing was created: rubbing MOVED electrons from the cloth to the
        rod. The cloth is left with an equal deficit, hence an equal and opposite charge. This is
        conservation of charge stated as a count rather than as a slogan.
    (c) Opposite signs, so attractive.
          F = k|q_1 q_2|/r^2 = (8.99e9)(8.0e-9)(8.0e-9)/(0.15)^2
          |q_1 q_2| = 6.4e-17 C^2
          k|q_1 q_2| = 5.7536e-7 N*m^2
          r^2 = 0.0225 m^2
          F = 5.7536e-7 / 0.0225 = 2.5572e-5 N = 2.6e-5 N = 26 microN, attractive.
  Pass 2 (re-derived, each part by a different route):
    (a) Back-substitute: (4.9938e10)(1.602e-19 C) = 8.000e-9 C. Recovers the given charge. Confirms.
    (c) Group the constants differently: k/r^2 = 8.99e9 / 0.0225 = 3.9956e11 N/C^2, times
        6.4e-17 C^2 = 2.5572e-5 N. Confirms.
  Final answer: (a) ~5.0e10 excess electrons. (b) The same ~5.0e10, transferred from the cloth;
  charge was moved, not made. (c) 2.6e-5 N, attractive.
Calibration: Exercises probe topics 1 and 2; difficulty standard; expected solve time ~4 min. Part
  (b) is the conceptual core and takes ten seconds if the cadet has the transfer model and cannot be
  answered at all without it.

C — Induction, and the order of operations
Statement: Two identical neutral metal spheres, A and B, rest on insulating stands and are touching
  each other. A NEGATIVELY charged rod is brought close to sphere A without touching it.
  (a) With the rod still held in place, what is the sign of the charge on the side of A nearest the
      rod, and on the far side of B?
  (b) Sphere B is now moved well away, and only then is the rod removed. What is the final charge on
      A and on B?
  (c) Suppose instead the rod is removed FIRST, and only afterwards is B moved away. What are the
      final charges?
  (d) A classmate says the rod must have given up some of its charge in part (b). Are they right?
Worked answer (tutor reference only):
  Pass 1:
    (a) A and B in contact form ONE conductor. The rod is negative, so it REPELS the conduction
        electrons, pushing them as far away as they can get — into B. So A's near side is left
        electron-poor and is POSITIVE; B's far side is electron-rich and is NEGATIVE.
    (b) Separating B while the rod is still holding the electrons over there traps them: B keeps the
        excess electrons and is NEGATIVE; A is left with the matching deficit and is POSITIVE. The
        two are equal in magnitude. Note the sphere nearest the rod ends up with the sign OPPOSITE
        to the rod's, which is the general signature of charging by induction.
    (c) Nothing. Remove the rod and the electrons are no longer being pushed, so they flow back and
        both spheres return to neutral. Separating two neutral spheres gives two neutral spheres.
        The ORDER is the entire content of the procedure.
    (d) No. The rod never touched anything, so nothing crossed between the rod and the spheres. All
        that happened was a redistribution of electrons already inside the two-sphere conductor. The
        rod ends with exactly the charge it began with — which is what makes induction repeatable
        with the same rod.
  Pass 2 (checked two independent ways):
    Conservation check: the spheres started with total charge zero and were never touched by
    anything charged, so their total must still be zero afterwards. In (b), A = +Q and B = -Q sums to
    zero. Confirms. In (c), 0 and 0 sums to zero. Confirms.
    Sign check against the opposite case: with a POSITIVE rod the electrons are ATTRACTED toward the
    rod, so the near sphere becomes negative and the far one positive — the mirror image of (a) and
    (b) throughout. Both cases obey the same one-line rule, which is a stronger check than either
    case alone.
  Final answer: (a) A near side positive, B far side negative. (b) A positive, B negative, equal in
  magnitude. (c) Both neutral. (d) No — the rod is unchanged.
Calibration: Exercises probe topics 4 and 3; difficulty standard; expected solve time ~5 min. It is
  entirely qualitative, which makes it a good offer for a cadet who says they are "bad at the math"
  — there is nowhere to hide, because every answer is a reason.

D — How badly does the electric force beat gravity?
Statement: In the ground state of hydrogen the electron sits 5.29e-11 m from the proton.
  (a) Find the magnitude of the electric attraction between them.
  (b) Using m_proton = 1.67e-27 kg, m_electron = 9.11e-31 kg and G = 6.67e-11 N*m^2/kg^2, find the
      gravitational attraction between them.
  (c) By what factor does the electric force exceed the gravitational one?
  (d) If the electric force is that much stronger, why is it gravity and not electricity that holds
      the solar system together?
Worked answer (tutor reference only):
  Pass 1:
    (a) F_E = k e^2 / r^2 = (8.99e9)(1.602e-19)^2 / (5.29e-11)^2
          (1.602e-19)^2 = 2.5664e-38 C^2
          (5.29e-11)^2  = 2.7984e-21 m^2
          numerator = (8.99e9)(2.5664e-38) = 2.3072e-28
          F_E = 2.3072e-28 / 2.7984e-21 = 8.2447e-8 N, so 8.25e-8 N. (Attractive.)
    (b) F_G = G m_p m_e / r^2
          m_p m_e = (1.67e-27)(9.11e-31) = 1.5214e-57 kg^2
          numerator = (6.67e-11)(1.5214e-57) = 1.0148e-67
          F_G = 1.0148e-67 / 2.7984e-21 = 3.6262e-47 N.
    (c) F_E / F_G = 8.2447e-8 / 3.6262e-47 = 2.27e39. About 2 x 10^39.
    (d) Because charge comes in TWO signs and mass comes in only one. Bulk matter is electrically
        neutral to extraordinary precision, so at planetary distances the attractions and repulsions
        from its positive and negative charges very nearly cancel and almost nothing is left. Nothing
        cancels gravity: every scrap of mass pulls the same way, so gravitational contributions just
        accumulate. A force that is intrinsically feeble but never cancels beats one that is
        overwhelming but almost always does.
  Pass 2 (re-derived, and (c) re-derived symbolically so it does not depend on (a) or (b)):
    Do the ratio without ever computing either force, and without r:
      F_E/F_G = k e^2 / (G m_p m_e), because the 1/r^2 is common to both and cancels exactly.
      = 2.3072e-28 / 1.0148e-67 = 2.2737e39. Confirms the value AND proves the bonus point that the
      ratio is the same at every separation — the two forces fall off identically.
    F_G by a different grouping: G/r^2 = 6.67e-11 / 2.7984e-21 = 2.3835e10; times 1.5214e-57 gives
      3.6262e-47 N. Confirms.
    F_E is also confirmed by today's worked example, which gets 8.25e-8 N for the same two charges at
      the same separation.
  Final answer: (a) 8.25e-8 N. (b) 3.63e-47 N. (c) About 2.3e39. (d) Because charge cancels and mass
  does not.
Calibration: Exercises probe topic 2, and pays off the gravitational lateral connection; difficulty
  challenging; expected solve time ~7 min. Part (d) is the real problem — parts (a) to (c) are
  arithmetic a careful cadet will get. Offer this one to a cadet who has already asked how the two
  forces compare.
